uncited: Geometry Shader Processing is a family of object-order rendering techniques that generate geometric primitives (cubes, quads, lines, or strips) directly on the GPU from scalar or vector field data, submitting them to the rasterizer [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].

It solves the problem of dynamic volumetric visualization by avoiding CPU-side mesh generation and pre-computed vertex buffers, instead expanding point primitives into visible surface geometry within the graphics pipeline [S2, S3, unofficial].

Unlike [Voxels rasterized as geometry](27-voxels-rasterized-as-geometry.md) which may rely on static buffers or CPU culling, this family performs visibility culling and primitive generation in the geometry shader stage, optimizing memory usage by storing only compact voxel attributes (position, color, face flags) [S2, S3, unofficial].
**Primitive Generation**: Each occupied voxel or data element is represented by one or more geometric primitives.
**Coordinate Transformation**: Voxel indices $(i, j, k)$ are transformed into world space.
**Rasterization**: The generated primitives are transformed into clip space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix and rasterized.
**Culling**: To manage performance, frustum culling is applied to exclude voxels outside the camera view.
Originating from the introduction of the Geometry Shader in OpenGL 3.0, these techniques leverage the GPU's ability to generate and transform primitives on the fly.

They are widely used in scientific visualization for real-time volumetric data exploration, particle systems, and caustic rendering, where dynamic geometry generation is preferred over static mesh storage.
